case: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 14-month history of progressive shortness of breath on exertion and one episode of near-syncope while climbing stairs. Her father died of an undiagnosed cardiopulmonary illness at the age of 45 years. Oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. Physical examination shows a loud pulmonic component of the second heart sound, a lift at the left lower sternal border, and mild ankle edema. Echocardiography shows a dilated, hypertrophied right ventricle and a normal left ventricle. Right heart catheterization shows a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 46 mm Hg (normal about 14; pulmonary hypertension is above 20), a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 9 mm Hg (normal 6 to 12), and increased pulmonary vascular resistance. CT angiography and a ventilation-perfusion scan show no emboli or lung disease. Diagnosis: heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension.

questions.stem: Genetic testing shows a heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in BMPR2, the gene most often mutated in heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension. Which of the following best describes the normal function of the protein encoded by this gene?
options: A G protein-coupled receptor for endothelin-1 that drives vasoconstriction
An extracellular microfibril protein that holds TGF-beta inactive in the vessel wall
A serine/threonine kinase receptor that restrains vascular smooth muscle growth
A receptor tyrosine kinase for PDGF that promotes smooth muscle proliferation
approach: Recognize BMPR2 as bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2, a member of the TGF-beta receptor family.
Recall that TGF-beta family receptors are serine/threonine kinases that signal through SMAD proteins.
Link loss of this growth-restraining signal to cell proliferation in small pulmonary arteries.
questions.why: BMPR2 encodes bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2, a serine/threonine kinase receptor in the TGF-beta superfamily. Its SMAD signaling normally inhibits proliferation of pulmonary vascular smooth muscle and supports endothelial survival. With one working copy lost, endothelial and smooth muscle cells proliferate, thickening the media and intima of small pulmonary arteries and raising resistance. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, so many carriers never develop disease.
whyNot: Endothelin-1 constricts and remodels pulmonary vessels and is high in this disease, but its receptors are G protein-coupled receptors and are not encoded by BMPR2.
This describes fibrillin-1. FBN1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, with aortic root dilation and dissection.
Correct.
PDGF does drive smooth muscle growth in pulmonary hypertension, but it acts through a receptor tyrosine kinase. BMPR2 signaling normally opposes this growth.

questions.stem: During a commercial airline flight, the reduced cabin pressure lowers her alveolar oxygen tension, and her shortness of breath worsens. Which of the following events in pulmonary arteriolar smooth muscle initiates the vascular response to alveolar hypoxia?
options: Inhibition of oxygen-sensitive K+ channels, depolarizing the cell
Opening of ATP-sensitive K+ channels, hyperpolarizing the cell
More nitric oxide release, raising cGMP and lowering cytosolic calcium
Adenosine binding A2A receptors, raising cyclic AMP in the cell
approach: Recall that alveolar hypoxia constricts pulmonary arterioles, the opposite of the dilation seen in most systemic arterioles.
Constriction needs a rise in cytosolic calcium, which follows membrane depolarization.
Pick the option that depolarizes the cell: closing potassium channels.
questions.why: Pulmonary arterioles constrict when alveolar oxygen falls, which normally diverts blood toward better-ventilated alveoli. Hypoxia inhibits oxygen-sensitive potassium channels in the smooth muscle, the membrane depolarizes, voltage-gated L-type calcium channels open, and calcium entry triggers contraction. At altitude the whole lung is hypoxic, so the constriction is widespread and adds to a pulmonary vascular resistance that is already high in her disease.
whyNot: Correct.
This is how hypoxia dilates many systemic arterioles, such as those in skeletal muscle and the heart. Hyperpolarization closes calcium channels and relaxes the cell.
Nitric oxide and cGMP relax smooth muscle. Hypoxia does not raise this pathway, and reduced nitric oxide signaling is part of the problem in pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Adenosine is a key metabolic vasodilator in the coronary circulation during hypoxia. Rising cyclic AMP relaxes vascular smooth muscle.

topics: Pulmonary and systemic responses to hypoxia

questions.stem: The lift on her anterior chest wall is palpated best at the left lower sternal border. Which of the following anatomic features best explains why enlargement of the affected chamber is palpable at this site?
options: The left ventricle forms the apex and most of the left border
The right atrium forms the right border of the heart shadow
The left atrium forms most of the base on the posterior surface
The right ventricle forms most of the sternocostal surface
approach: Identify the chamber under strain: pulmonary hypertension loads the right ventricle.
Recall which chamber faces the anterior chest wall.
Match the right ventricle to the left parasternal location of the heave.
questions.why: Pulmonary hypertension raises right ventricular afterload, so the right ventricle hypertrophies and dilates. The right ventricle lies just behind the sternum and left parasternal region and forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart. A forceful, enlarged right ventricle therefore lifts the chest wall at the left lower sternal border, called a parasternal heave.
whyNot: Left ventricular enlargement moves the apex beat down and to the left, near or beyond the left midclavicular line. Her left ventricle is normal.
The right atrium forms the right heart border on a frontal chest film. It does not lie under the left lower sternum.
The left atrium forms the base and lies against the esophagus. When it enlarges, as in mitral stenosis, it can push the esophagus back, but it cannot be felt on the front of the chest.
Correct.

topics: Surfaces and borders of the heart

questions.stem: Two years later, she dies of progressive right-sided heart failure. Which of the following findings in the lungs at autopsy is most characteristic of her disease?
options: Hemosiderin-laden macrophages filling the alveolar spaces
Plexiform lesions in small muscular pulmonary arteries
Hyaline membranes lining the alveolar ducts
Noncaseating granulomas along bronchovascular bundles
approach: Classify her disease as precapillary: high pulmonary artery pressure with a normal wedge pressure.
Recall the vascular changes of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Rule out lesions that point to left heart failure, acute alveolar injury, or granulomatous lung disease.
questions.why: Severe pulmonary arterial hypertension remodels small muscular pulmonary arteries and arterioles with medial hypertrophy and intimal fibrosis, and in advanced idiopathic and heritable disease it produces plexiform lesions. A plexiform lesion is a tuft of small, slit-like capillary channels inside a dilated arterial segment, formed by proliferating endothelial cells. It reflects the uncontrolled endothelial and smooth muscle growth that follows loss of BMPR2 signaling.
whyNot: These heart failure cells form when high left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure leaks red cells into the alveoli, as in chronic left heart failure or mitral stenosis. Her normal wedge pressure rules out that cause.
Correct.
Hyaline membranes mark diffuse alveolar damage, as in acute respiratory distress syndrome. They reflect acute injury to the alveolar wall.
Noncaseating granulomas suggest sarcoidosis, which can cause pulmonary hypertension through lung fibrosis. Her imaging showed no lung disease, and granulomas are not a feature of heritable disease.

dx: Systemic hypertension with concentric left ventricular hypertrophy
case: A 58-year-old man who works as a delivery truck driver comes to the physician for a required work physical examination. He was diagnosed with hypertension 12 years ago but stopped treatment many years ago. He reports mild shortness of breath when climbing two flights of stairs. Blood pressure is 174/104 mm Hg on repeated measurements. Physical examination shows a sustained, nondisplaced apical impulse and a fourth heart sound at the apex. An ECG shows increased QRS voltage with a left ventricular strain pattern. Echocardiography shows concentric hypertrophy with an interventricular septal thickness of 15 mm (normal 6 to 10), normal chamber size, an ejection fraction of 62% (normal 52 to 72%), and impaired relaxation. Serum creatinine concentration is 1.1 mg/dL (normal 0.7 to 1.3). Diagnosis: hypertensive heart disease with concentric left ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.stem: One year later, he develops atrial fibrillation. With medication, his ventricular rate is maintained at about 75/min, but his exercise tolerance decreases further and the fourth heart sound is no longer heard. Loss of which of the following phases of the cardiac cycle best explains this decline?
options: Atrial systole at the end of ventricular filling
Rapid ventricular filling just after mitral opening
Isovolumetric relaxation before the mitral valve opens
Reduced ejection late in ventricular systole
approach: Note what changed: atrial fibrillation with a controlled rate, so a short diastole is not the explanation.
Recall that the fourth heart sound comes from atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle.
Conclude that a stiff ventricle relies on atrial systole for filling, which atrial fibrillation removes.
questions.why: A stiff, concentrically hypertrophied left ventricle fills poorly in early diastole, so it depends more on atrial contraction at the end of diastole. In a normal heart the atrial kick adds about 20 percent of filling, and in a stiff ventricle its share is larger. Atrial fibrillation removes organized atrial contraction, so end-diastolic volume and stroke volume fall. The fourth heart sound is made by atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, which is why it disappears.
whyNot: Correct.

Rapid filling still happens in atrial fibrillation because it is driven by the pressure gradient when the mitral valve opens. It was already reduced by his impaired relaxation and does not explain the new decline.
Isovolumetric relaxation still occurs with every beat, and no blood enters the ventricle during it. Slow relaxation in this phase is part of his baseline disease.
Ejection depends on ventricular contraction, which continues in atrial fibrillation. This phase is not lost.

questions.stem: Echocardiography shows slowed early diastolic relaxation. Myocardial relaxation requires ATP and is delayed when myocardial ATP is depleted. Which of the following steps in the cross-bridge cycle directly detaches the myosin head from actin?
options: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate on the myosin head
Release of phosphate, which triggers the power stroke
Release of ADP at the end of the power stroke
Binding of an ATP molecule to the myosin head
approach: Picture the head after the power stroke: attached to actin with no nucleotide (the rigor state).
Ask what must happen for it to let go: a new ATP must bind.
Keep the roles apart: binding detaches, hydrolysis recocks, phosphate release powers the stroke.
questions.why: After the power stroke, a myosin head bound to actin with no nucleotide is in the rigor state. Binding of a new ATP molecule lowers myosin's affinity for actin, and the head detaches. Hydrolysis of that ATP then recocks the head for the next cycle. When ATP is scarce, as in energy-starved hypertrophied muscle, heads stay attached longer and relaxation slows. Rigor mortis is the extreme case, with no ATP left to release the heads.
whyNot: Hydrolysis happens after detachment and recocks the head into its high-energy position. The head is already free of actin at this step.
Phosphate release strengthens binding to actin and starts the power stroke. It moves the filaments and does not separate them.
ADP release ends the power stroke and leaves the head tightly bound to actin in the rigor state. A new ATP must bind before the head can let go.
Correct.

questions.stem: He later reports pressure-like chest discomfort that occurs with heavy exertion and resolves within minutes of rest. Coronary angiography shows no significant stenosis of the epicardial arteries. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his exertional ischemia?
options: Rupture of a small plaque with a nonocclusive thrombus
Myocyte mass outgrowing its capillary supply
Spasm of a large epicardial coronary artery
Vasculitis narrowing small coronary arteries
approach: Note the clues: exertional pain, thick ventricle, clean epicardial arteries.
Compare oxygen supply and demand in a hypertrophied wall.
Choose the mechanism tied to hypertrophy itself.
questions.why: In concentric hypertrophy, myocytes enlarge but capillary density does not keep pace, so the distance oxygen must diffuse increases. Oxygen demand rises with the larger muscle mass and high systolic wall stress. A thick, stiff wall with high diastolic pressure also compresses subendocardial vessels, which fill mainly in diastole. During exertion, demand outruns supply and the subendocardium becomes ischemic even with normal epicardial arteries.
whyNot: Plaque rupture with thrombus causes unstable angina or infarction, and angiography would show a culprit lesion. His arteries are clear.
Correct.
Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina typically occurs at rest, often in the early morning, and is not reliably brought on by exertion.
Vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa or Kawasaki disease can damage coronary arteries, but he has no systemic features, and his symptoms track with the work of a thickened ventricle.

questions.stem: Eight years later, still untreated, he has the sudden onset of right-sided weakness and slurred speech. CT of the head shows a hemorrhage in the left putamen and internal capsule. Rupture of which of the following vessels most likely caused this hemorrhage?
options: Bridging veins crossing the subdural space
A saccular aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery
Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery
The middle meningeal artery beneath the pterion
approach: Locate the bleed: putamen and internal capsule, deep in the brain.
Recall which arteries supply that region: lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery.
Link chronic hypertension to damage in small penetrating arteries.
questions.why: Long-standing hypertension damages small penetrating arteries and can form tiny microaneurysms in their walls. The lenticulostriate arteries arise from the first part of the middle cerebral artery and enter the brain to supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule. Their rupture causes intraparenchymal hemorrhage, and the putamen is the most common site of hypertensive hemorrhage. Damage to the internal capsule produces weakness on the opposite side of the body.
whyNot: Torn bridging veins cause a subdural hematoma, usually after head trauma in older adults or people with brain atrophy. Blood collects over the brain surface.
A ruptured berry aneurysm causes subarachnoid hemorrhage with a sudden, severe headache. Blood fills the subarachnoid space around the circle of Willis.
Correct.
A torn middle meningeal artery follows a skull fracture at the pterion and causes an epidural hematoma, often with a lucid interval.

topics: Blood supply of the basal ganglia and internal capsule

dx: Renovascular hypertension from atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis
case: A 66-year-old woman is referred to the physician because of a blood pressure of 182/98 mm Hg despite treatment with three antihypertensive medications. Her blood pressure was normal until the age of 62 years. She has peripheral artery disease and has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Physical examination shows an epigastric bruit. Funduscopic examination shows arteriolar narrowing without papilledema. Serum potassium concentration is 3.2 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0), serum creatinine concentration is 1.3 mg/dL (normal 0.6 to 1.1), and plasma renin activity is increased. Ultrasonography shows a right kidney 8.6 cm long and a left kidney 11.2 cm long (normal 10 to 12). CT angiography shows an 80% stenosis at the origin of the right renal artery caused by an atherosclerotic plaque. Diagnosis: renovascular hypertension due to right renal artery stenosis.

questions.stem: Assume that flow through the stenosis is laminar and follows Poiseuille's law. If the luminal radius at the stenosis is half its normal value, with length, viscosity, and all other factors unchanged, resistance in that segment increases by approximately which of the following factors?
options: 4-fold
8-fold
16-fold
32-fold
approach: Write Poiseuille's law: resistance = 8 x viscosity x length / (pi x radius to the fourth power).
Halve the radius: radius to the fourth power falls to 1/16.
Resistance therefore rises 16-fold.
questions.why: Poiseuille's law states that resistance is proportional to vessel length and blood viscosity and inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius. Halving the radius raises resistance by 2 to the fourth power, which is 16. This is why a moderate narrowing can sharply cut flow and pressure beyond it, and why the kidney beyond a tight stenosis senses low perfusion pressure.
whyNot: A 4-fold rise would follow if resistance depended on cross-sectional area (radius squared). Poiseuille's law uses the fourth power.
An 8-fold rise would follow from the third power of the radius, which does not appear in Poiseuille's law.
Correct.
A 32-fold rise would need a fifth-power relationship. Resistance varies with the fourth power of the radius.

questions.stem: Decreased perfusion pressure distal to the stenosis is sensed within the right kidney and stimulates renin release. Which of the following cells secretes the renin?
options: Podocytes on the outer surface of glomerular capillaries
Macula densa cells in the wall of the distal tubule
Interstitial fibroblasts near the peritubular capillaries
Modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole
approach: Connect the clue (low pressure in the renal arterial tree) to the renin-angiotensin system.
Recall the juxtaglomerular apparatus and which of its parts stores renin.
Place the juxtaglomerular cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole.
questions.why: Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole near the glomerular vascular pole. They store renin in granules and release it when stretch in the arteriole falls, when the macula densa senses low sodium chloride delivery, and with sympathetic beta-1 stimulation. In renal artery stenosis, low afferent arteriolar pressure in the affected kidney increases renin, which raises angiotensin II and aldosterone. Excess aldosterone explains her low potassium.
whyNot: Podocytes form the filtration slits of the glomerular barrier. They do not make renin.
Macula densa cells sense sodium chloride in the tubular fluid and signal the juxtaglomerular cells, but they do not secrete renin themselves.
Peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in the cortex make erythropoietin in response to low oxygen delivery.
Correct.

questions.stem: The plaque at the origin of the renal artery contains many lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells). Which of the following features of macrophage lipid handling best explains why these cells continue to take up cholesterol until they are engorged?
options: Scavenger receptors for oxidized LDL escape feedback by cell cholesterol
LDL receptors increase as cell cholesterol rises, through SREBP activation
ABCA1 transporters move cholesterol from HDL into the macrophage
ACAT is inhibited, so free cholesterol cannot be stored as ester
approach: Recall how native LDL uptake is limited by feedback on the LDL receptor.
Note that LDL trapped in the intima is oxidized.
Identify the uptake route that lacks feedback control: scavenger receptors.
questions.why: Native LDL enters cells through the LDL receptor, and rising cell cholesterol shuts off SREBP and lowers LDL receptor numbers, which limits uptake. LDL trapped in the intima becomes oxidized. Macrophages take up oxidized LDL through scavenger receptors such as SR-A and CD36, and these receptors are not reduced as cholesterol builds up. ACAT stores the excess as cholesteryl ester droplets, which give the cells their foamy look.
whyNot: Correct.
SREBP is activated when cell cholesterol is low. High cell cholesterol suppresses LDL receptor synthesis, which limits native LDL uptake.
ABCA1 does the reverse: it exports cholesterol from the macrophage to apolipoprotein A-I to form HDL. Loss of ABCA1 (Tangier disease) causes cholesterol buildup in macrophages.
ACAT is active in foam cells. It esterifies cholesterol, and the stored cholesteryl ester droplets give the cells their foamy appearance.

questions.stem: Her hypertension has been present for about 4 years. Histologic examination of the left (unaffected) kidney would most likely show which of the following findings?
options: Ischemic atrophy with shrunken tubules and crowded glomeruli
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis from chronic high pressure
Hyperplastic onion-skin thickening with fibrinoid necrosis
Concentric ring-like calcification of the arteriolar media
approach: Note that the stenosis shields the right kidney from high pressure while the left kidney receives it in full.
Recall the arteriolar change of chronic, non-malignant hypertension.
Rule out malignant hypertension: no papilledema and pressures below that range.
questions.why: The stenosis protects the right kidney's small vessels from high pressure, while the left kidney receives the full systemic pressure. Over years, plasma proteins leak into the walls of its arterioles and smooth muscle cells lay down extra matrix, producing hyaline arteriolosclerosis. The arterioles narrow, and the kidney develops benign nephrosclerosis. The right kidney instead shrinks from ischemia, which matches its small size on ultrasound.
whyNot: Ischemic atrophy is the expected change in the right kidney, downstream of the stenosis, and it explains that kidney's small size.
Correct.
Onion-skin hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis marks malignant hypertension, usually with pressures above about 200/120 mm Hg and papilledema. She has neither.
Ring-like medial calcification describes Mönckeberg medial sclerosis, which affects medium-sized muscular arteries in older adults and does not narrow the lumen.

dx: Acute left-sided heart failure with pulmonary edema due to viral myocarditis
case: A 29-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of progressive shortness of breath. He cannot lie flat and is coughing up pink, frothy sputum. Two weeks ago, he had fever, sore throat, and diarrhea. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 98/64 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Physical examination shows crackles over both lung fields and a third heart sound. A chest x-ray shows bilateral perihilar alveolar opacities and Kerley B lines. Serum troponin I concentration is increased. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25% (normal 52 to 72%). Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is 28 mm Hg (normal 6 to 12). Diagnosis: acute left-sided heart failure with pulmonary edema due to viral myocarditis.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes in the forces across the pulmonary capillary wall is the primary cause of the fluid in his alveoli?
options: Fall in plasma colloid osmotic pressure
Rise in pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
Rise in capillary permeability to plasma proteins
Blockage of lymph drainage from the lung interstitium
approach: Read the wedge pressure: 28 mm Hg means high left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure.
Apply the Starling forces: high capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out.
Separate cardiogenic edema (high wedge pressure) from permeability edema (normal wedge pressure).
questions.why: Pulmonary capillary pressure is normally about 7 mm Hg, well below the plasma colloid osmotic pressure of about 28 mm Hg, so the lungs stay dry. A failing left ventricle raises left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure, shown by his wedge pressure of 28 mm Hg. When capillary pressure reaches the colloid osmotic pressure and lymph flow can no longer keep up, fluid fills the interstitium (Kerley B lines) and then the alveoli.
whyNot: Low oncotic pressure from low albumin, as in nephrotic syndrome or cirrhosis, favors edema, but nothing suggests low albumin here, and his wedge pressure explains the edema.
Correct.
Increased permeability causes noncardiogenic edema, as in acute respiratory distress syndrome or sepsis. In that setting the wedge pressure is not elevated.
Lymphatic blockage, as from tumor spread, causes interstitial fluid buildup. His lymphatics are working and are simply overwhelmed.

questions.stem: PCR of an endomyocardial biopsy specimen detects coxsackievirus B3 RNA. Which of the following best describes this virus and its most likely route of transmission to this patient?
options: Enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA, spread by respiratory droplets
Nonenveloped, double-stranded DNA, spread by droplets and fomites
Enveloped, double-stranded DNA, spread by close contact with saliva
Nonenveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA, spread fecal-orally
approach: Place coxsackievirus in its family: an enterovirus within the picornaviruses.
Recall picornavirus structure: small, nonenveloped, positive-sense RNA.
Match the route to his diarrheal prodrome: fecal-oral.
questions.why: Coxsackievirus B is an enterovirus in the picornavirus family. It is small and nonenveloped, with a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome that can be translated directly as mRNA. Without an envelope it survives stomach acid and spreads mainly by the fecal-oral route, which fits his diarrheal illness two weeks earlier. It enters cardiac myocytes through the coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor (CAR).
whyNot: This describes influenza, which spreads by droplets and can occasionally cause myocarditis. It is not an enterovirus.
This describes adenovirus, another cause of viral myocarditis, especially in children. It is a DNA virus.
This describes herpesviruses such as Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus, which spread through saliva and other close contact.
Correct.

questions.stem: His wedge pressure was measured with a balloon-tipped catheter advanced into a small branch of the pulmonary artery and inflated until flow stopped. Which of the following best explains why this measurement approximates his left ventricular filling pressure?
options: The catheter tip senses pressure in the bronchial arteries
The balloon transmits right ventricular pressure forward
A still column of blood links the tip to the left atrium
The tip lies in a pulmonary vein beside the left atrium
approach: Trace the path from a pulmonary artery branch through capillaries and pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
Apply the rule that with no flow there is no pressure drop along a vessel.
Link left atrial pressure to left ventricular pressure in diastole through the open mitral valve.
questions.why: Inflating the balloon blocks flow in that branch. With no flow there is no pressure drop along the vessels downstream, so the blood in the capillaries and pulmonary veins forms a static column connected to the left atrium. The tip therefore reads left atrial pressure. In diastole the mitral valve is open, so left atrial pressure approximates left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, unless a problem such as mitral stenosis separates them.
whyNot: Bronchial arteries come from the systemic circulation (the aorta or intercostal arteries) and supply the airways. The catheter lies in a pulmonary artery branch.
The inflated balloon blocks the pressure coming from the right ventricle. Before inflation the catheter reads pulmonary artery pressure.
Correct.
The catheter stays in the pulmonary artery tree and cannot pass through the capillaries. It reflects venous pressure only through the static column of blood.

questions.stem: The biopsy specimen also shows lymphocytes infiltrating the myocardium adjacent to necrotic myocytes. The infected myocytes display viral peptides on their surface. Which of the following immune mechanisms most directly kills these infected myocytes?
options: CD8 T cells binding viral peptide on MHC class I
CD4 T cells recognizing viral peptide on MHC class I
IgE on mast cells triggering histamine release
Immune complexes depositing in small vessel walls
approach: Note that viral proteins made inside the myocyte are presented on MHC class I.
Recall which T cells recognize MHC class I: CD8 cytotoxic T cells.
Link the lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis to cell-mediated killing.
questions.why: Cardiac myocytes, like nearly all nucleated cells, present peptides from viral proteins made in their cytoplasm on MHC class I. Cytotoxic CD8 T cells recognize these complexes and kill the cell with perforin and granzymes or Fas ligand. This clears the virus but also destroys myocytes, and a lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis is the hallmark of viral myocarditis. Loss of myocytes weakens contraction and leads to acute left heart failure.
whyNot: Correct.
CD4 T cells recognize peptide on MHC class II, found mainly on antigen-presenting cells. They help the response but do not directly kill infected myocytes.
IgE on mast cells drives type I hypersensitivity, such as anaphylaxis and allergic asthma. It plays no direct part in killing virus-infected myocytes.
Immune complex deposition (type III hypersensitivity) causes vasculitis, as in serum sickness or lupus. It inflames vessel walls and does not target infected myocytes.

topics: MHC class I and cytotoxic T cells

dx: Right-sided heart failure (cor pulmonale) due to cystic fibrosis lung disease
case: A 24-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis (homozygous for F508del) comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of ankle swelling, abdominal fullness, and fatigue. She has advanced lung disease with chronic airway infection by a mucoid gram-negative rod, and her FEV1 is 28% of predicted. Physical examination shows jugular venous distention to 7 cm above the sternal angle (normal 3 cm or less), a loud pulmonic component of the second heart sound, a tender, enlarged liver, and pitting edema to the mid-shins. On room air, arterial PO2 is 54 mm Hg (normal 80 to 100). Hematocrit is 52% (normal 36 to 46), and serum ALT activity is 88 U/L (normal 7 to 35). Echocardiography shows a dilated right ventricle, a flattened septum, and normal left ventricular function. Diagnosis: right-sided heart failure (cor pulmonale) due to cystic fibrosis lung disease.

questions.stem: Her F508del mutation deletes one phenylalanine residue from the CFTR protein. Which of the following best explains the loss of CFTR function in her airway epithelial cells?
options: A premature stop codon that produces a short, truncated protein
A protein that reaches the cell membrane but rarely opens its channel
A misfolded protein held in the endoplasmic reticulum and degraded
A promoter mutation that sharply lowers transcription of the gene
approach: Note the mutation type: an in-frame deletion of one amino acid.
Recall what happens to misfolded membrane proteins: endoplasmic reticulum quality control and proteasomal degradation.
Connect the missing chloride channel to thick mucus, chronic lung disease, and pulmonary hypertension.
questions.why: F508del is an in-frame deletion of three nucleotides that removes phenylalanine at position 508. The protein misfolds, is caught by quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum, and is degraded by the proteasome, so little CFTR reaches the apical membrane (a class II processing defect). Without this chloride channel, airway surface liquid becomes dehydrated and mucus thickens, leading to chronic infection, bronchiectasis, hypoxemia, and eventually pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
whyNot: Nonsense mutations such as G542X create a premature stop codon (class I). F508del removes one amino acid and keeps the reading frame.
Gating mutations such as G551D (class III) produce a protein that reaches the membrane but opens poorly.
Correct.
Promoter or splicing mutations reduce the amount of normal protein made. F508del leaves transcription intact and changes how the protein folds.

topics: Protein folding and ER quality control

questions.stem: Her mucoid gram-negative rod is oxidase positive, produces a blue-green pigment, and has persisted for years despite a dense neutrophilic infiltrate in her airways. Which of the following bacterial products best explains this persistence?
options: Exotoxin A, which ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2
Alginate, which forms a protective biofilm matrix
Lipid A, which binds Toll-like receptor 4
Flagellin, which drives motility through airway mucus
approach: Identify the organism: an oxidase-positive, pigment-making, mucoid gram-negative rod in cystic fibrosis is Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Ask which product shields bacteria from phagocytes over the long term.
Choose the exopolysaccharide that defines the mucoid form: alginate.
questions.why: The organism is Pseudomonas aeruginosa. In the cystic fibrosis lung it switches to a mucoid form that overproduces alginate, an exopolysaccharide. Alginate builds a biofilm that blocks phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages, scavenges oxidants, and limits antibody and antibiotic penetration. Neutrophils keep arriving but cannot clear the bacteria, and their proteases and oxidants damage the airways, driving bronchiectasis, hypoxemia, and pulmonary hypertension.
whyNot: Exotoxin A blocks host protein synthesis and kills tissue cells, much like diphtheria toxin. It damages tissue but does not shield the bacteria from clearance.
Correct.
Lipid A is the toxic part of endotoxin. It activates TLR4 and drives inflammation and septic shock, which helps the host detect the bacteria.
Flagellin is detected by TLR5, and Pseudomonas from chronic cystic fibrosis infection often loses its flagella, which helps it avoid detection.

questions.stem: Her jugular venous pressure is assessed using the right internal jugular vein with the head of the bed elevated to 45 degrees. Which of the following best explains why this vein is preferred for estimating right atrial pressure?
options: It lines up almost straight with the SVC and right atrium
It drains straight into the right atrium through its own opening
It lies superficial to sternocleidomastoid, where it is easy to see
It reaches the heart by crossing the midline in front of the aorta
approach: Trace the venous path from the right internal jugular vein to the right atrium.
Note that a short, straight column transmits right atrial pressure best.
Rule out options that describe the external jugular or the left-sided veins.
questions.why: The right internal jugular vein joins the right subclavian vein to form the right brachiocephalic vein, which runs almost straight down into the superior vena cava (SVC) and right atrium. This short, direct path lets the height of the pulsating column reflect right atrial pressure. In right heart failure, rising right atrial pressure shows as distended neck veins. The external jugular vein is easier to see but takes a more angled course through the deep fascia, so it is less reliable.
whyNot: Correct.
No neck vein opens directly into the right atrium. Blood reaches it through the brachiocephalic veins and the SVC.
This describes the external jugular vein. The internal jugular lies deep to sternocleidomastoid, so its pulsation is seen as movement in the neck rather than as a visible vein.
This describes the left brachiocephalic vein, which carries left internal jugular blood across the midline. That longer route makes the left side less reliable.

topics: Veins of the neck and thorax

questions.stem: A liver biopsy specimen would most likely show which of the following patterns?
options: Fatty change with large lipid droplets in hepatocytes
Portal tract lymphocytes with interface hepatitis
Bile duct destruction by granulomas in portal tracts
Congestion and hepatocyte loss around central veins
approach: Trace back-pressure from the right atrium through the inferior vena cava and hepatic veins to the central veins.
Recall that the central (zone 3) hepatocytes are also the least oxygenated.
Choose congestion and injury around central veins.
questions.why: Right heart failure raises right atrial pressure, which passes back through the inferior vena cava and hepatic veins into the central veins of the liver lobules. Blood pools around the central veins (zone 3), the zone farthest from the oxygen-rich portal inflow. Hepatocytes there atrophy and may die, while better-oxygenated periportal cells survive. The dark, congested centers against paler surrounding tissue give the cut liver a nutmeg look.
whyNot: Fatty change (steatosis) comes from alcohol, obesity, insulin resistance, or other metabolic causes. It does not reflect venous congestion and would not explain a tender, swollen liver with distended neck veins.
Interface hepatitis with portal lymphocytes is the pattern of chronic viral or autoimmune hepatitis.
Granulomatous bile duct destruction is the classic lesion of primary biliary cholangitis.
Correct.

topics: Chronic passive congestion of the liver

dx: Chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction from Chagas cardiomyopathy, with neurohormonal activation
case: A 54-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive fatigue, shortness of breath after walking one block, and leg swelling. He moved to the United States from rural Bolivia 25 years ago. Pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows bibasilar crackles, a third heart sound, and pitting edema of the legs. An ECG shows right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle, an ejection fraction of 27% (normal 52 to 72%), and a small apical aneurysm. Serum BNP is 1,240 pg/mL (normal less than 100), sodium 130 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145), and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (normal 0.7 to 1.3). IgG antibodies to Trypanosoma cruzi are positive on two assays. Diagnosis: Chagas cardiomyopathy with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

questions.stem: He most likely acquired the infection during childhood. Which of the following is the usual route of transmission of this organism to humans in endemic areas?
options: Bite of an infected female sandfly
Bite of an infected tsetse fly
Bite of an infected Anopheles mosquito
Feces of an infected triatomine bug
approach: Identify the organism from the serology: Trypanosoma cruzi, the cause of Chagas disease.
Recall its vector: the triatomine (reduviid, kissing) bug.
Note that the parasite passes in the bug's feces during or after the blood meal.
questions.why: Trypanosoma cruzi is carried by triatomine (reduviid, or kissing) bugs that feed at night, often on the face. The bug defecates while feeding, and trypomastigotes in its feces enter through the bite wound or the conjunctiva when the person rubs the area. Inside host cells, including cardiac myocytes, the parasite multiplies as amastigotes. Decades later, about 20 to 30 percent of infected people develop chronic heart disease. Blood transfusion, organ transplant, mother-to-child spread, and contaminated food are less common routes.
whyNot: Sandflies transmit Leishmania, which causes cutaneous or visceral leishmaniasis.
Tsetse flies transmit Trypanosoma brucei, the cause of African sleeping sickness. That parasite passes in the fly's saliva during the bite.
Anopheles mosquitoes transmit Plasmodium species, the cause of malaria.
Correct.

questions.stem: Myocytes from failing hearts such as his show smaller calcium transients with each beat and slower removal of calcium from the cytosol. Which of the following changes most directly reduces the calcium available for each contraction?
options: Lower SERCA2a activity refilling the sarcoplasmic reticulum
More phospholamban phosphorylation by protein kinase A
Less sodium-calcium exchange, trapping calcium in the cytosol
Tighter closure of ryanodine receptors during diastole
approach: Recall that each beat releases calcium stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Ask which pump refills that store: SERCA2a.
Link less refilling to smaller release, weaker contraction, and slower relaxation.
questions.why: With each beat, calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum through ryanodine receptors binds troponin C. Relaxation and the next beat depend on SERCA2a pumping that calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. In heart failure, SERCA2a expression and activity fall, and its inhibitor phospholamban is less phosphorylated, so it inhibits SERCA2a more. Less calcium is stored, less is released with the next beat, and contraction weakens. Slower reuptake also slows relaxation.
whyNot: Correct.

Protein kinase A phosphorylation of phospholamban relieves its inhibition of SERCA2a and raises stored calcium, as during sympathetic stimulation. In failing hearts phospholamban phosphorylation is reduced.
The sodium-calcium exchanger is increased in failing myocytes and removes more calcium from the cell. If exchange were reduced, more calcium would stay in the cell.
In heart failure, ryanodine receptors tend to leak calcium during diastole, which further drains the stores. Tighter closure would preserve them.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the change in his left ventricular pressure-volume loop compared with that of a healthy adult?
options: Steeper end-diastolic curve, normal end-systolic volume
No isovolumetric relaxation, with a much wider loop
Flatter end-systolic line, loop at larger volumes
Narrower loop shifted to a smaller end-diastolic volume
approach: Identify the primary defect: reduced contractility (ejection fraction 27%).
Recall that contractility is shown by the slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume line.
Predict the result: larger end-systolic and end-diastolic volumes, with a small stroke volume.
questions.why: Contractility is shown by the slope of the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship. In systolic heart failure that slope falls, so at any afterload the ventricle empties less and end-systolic volume rises. The ventricle dilates and end-diastolic volume rises as the body retains fluid to raise preload. The loop moves to the right and becomes narrow, because stroke volume is small compared with the large end-diastolic volume, giving his ejection fraction of 27%.
whyNot: A steep end-diastolic curve with normal systolic function describes a stiff ventricle, as in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction from hypertensive hypertrophy.
Loss of a true isovolumetric relaxation phase occurs in aortic regurgitation, because blood leaks back into the ventricle as soon as ejection ends. That loop widens from a large stroke volume.
Correct.
A narrow loop at small volumes reflects low preload, as in hemorrhage or dehydration. His ventricle is dilated.

questions.stem: His serum sodium concentration is 130 mEq/L although his total body sodium is increased. Which of the following hormones most directly causes the low serum sodium concentration?
options: Aldosterone acting on collecting duct principal cells
Vasopressin acting on collecting duct V2 receptors
Norepinephrine acting on renal tubular alpha-1 receptors
Cortisol acting on renal mineralocorticoid receptors
approach: Recognize hyponatremia with volume overload as a sign of excess free water.
Ask which hormone adds free water: vasopressin (ADH).
Explain its release despite low osmolality: baroreceptors sense low effective arterial volume.
questions.why: In heart failure, low cardiac output reduces effective arterial blood volume. Arterial baroreceptors sense this and trigger nonosmotic release of vasopressin (ADH), which overrides the normal suppression of ADH by low plasma osmolality. Vasopressin binds V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells and inserts aquaporin-2 channels, so free water is reabsorbed. Water retained in excess of sodium dilutes plasma sodium. Low serum sodium in heart failure signals strong neurohormonal activation and a worse prognosis.
whyNot: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption, and water follows, which expands volume and causes edema. On its own it does not dilute plasma sodium, and it also increases potassium secretion.
Correct.
Norepinephrine raises heart rate, contractility, renin release, and tubular sodium reabsorption, which adds to fluid retention. It does not directly add free water.
At high levels cortisol can act on mineralocorticoid receptors and retain sodium, which tends to keep sodium up. Low sodium is a feature of cortisol deficiency, through increased vasopressin.
